    tenable.com · 14 Jul 2026 18:23 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.5

    In plain words

    Microsoft released its largest-ever monthly security update, fixing 569 problems across Windows, Microsoft Office, SharePoint, Dynamics, Active Directory services, and many other Microsoft products. Two of the problems had already been used by attackers before the fixes were available, including issues in Active Directory Federation Services and SharePoint Server. This matters because some of these flaws could let attackers gain administrator-level control or run harmful commands on affected systems, so organizations using these products need to apply the updates quickly.

    Summary
    Microsoft’s July 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes a record 569 CVEs, including three zero-days and two vulnerabilities already exploited in the wild affecting Active Directory Federation Services and SharePoint Server. Organizations should prioritize patching the exploited zero-days and critical flaws in Dynamics, DHCP, and Windows Kernel components.

    Microsoft patched 569 CVEs in its July 2026 Patch Tuesday release, making it the largest Patch Tuesday release to date. The update includes 56 critical, 510 important, and 3 moderate vulnerabilities. Microsoft said customers should expect a higher volume of security updates as its multi-model agentic scanning harness is being used to identify vulnerabilities faster.

    The release includes three zero-days, two of which were exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-56155 affects Active Directory Federation Services and could allow an attacker to gain administrator privileges, while CVE-2026-56164 affects Microsoft SharePoint Server and was also exploited in the wild. Microsoft also patched CVE-2026-50661, a publicly disclosed Windows BitLocker security feature bypass vulnerability that requires physical access to exploit.

    Several critical issues were highlighted, including CVE-2026-55944 in Microsoft Dynamics NAV and Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central, which can be exploited without authentication or user interaction through a crafted login request. Microsoft also addressed nine DHCP Server and Windows DHCP Client vulnerabilities, five of which were rated critical. Elevation of privilege vulnerabilities accounted for 43.8% of the flaws patched this month, and Windows Kernel received 20 elevation of privilege fixes.

    • The record-breaking number of fixes appears tied to Microsoft’s use of its multi-model agentic scanning harness, with Microsoft warning customers to expect higher volumes of security updates in each release.
    • The Microsoft Dynamics NAV and Dynamics 365 Business Central vulnerability is especially actionable because Microsoft says exploitation requires neither authentication nor user interaction and can be triggered with a crafted login request.
    • For the exploited SharePoint Server vulnerability, Microsoft specifically identifies AMSI integration as a mitigation that can scan for and detect malicious POST requests.
    • Although CVE-2026-50661 has a public exploit, Microsoft assesses exploitation as less likely because an attacker needs physical access to the target device.
    • Elevation of privilege issues made up the largest share of the release at 43.8%, and the Windows Kernel alone received 20 elevation of privilege fixes, including six assessed as more likely to be exploited.
    Key Points
    • 01Microsoft patched 569 CVEs in its July 2026 Patch Tuesday release, with 56 rated critical, 510 rated important, and 3 rated moderate.
    • 02The July 2026 release includes three zero-days, two of which were exploited in the wild.
    • 03CVE-2026-56155 is an elevation of privilege vulnerability in Active Directory Federation Services that was exploited in the wild and could allow an attacker to gain administrator privileges.
    • 04CVE-2026-56164 is an elevation of privilege vulnerability in Microsoft SharePoint Server that was exploited in the wild and affects SharePoint Server 2019, SharePoint Server Subscription Edition, SharePoint Server 2016, and SharePoint Enterprise Server 2016.
    • 05Microsoft addressed multiple DHCP Server and Windows DHCP Client vulnerabilities, including five rated critical and three assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”

    In plain words

    Microsoft released its July 2026 security fixes for a record 570 problems across Windows and many Microsoft products, including issues in Active Directory Federation Services, SharePoint Server, BitLocker, Office, Exchange Server, SQL Server, Remote Desktop, and more. This matters because two of the problems were already being used in real attacks: one could let someone gain administrator-level access through Active Directory Federation Services, and another could let a remote attacker gain higher access through SharePoint Server. A third publicly known BitLocker problem could let someone with physical access to a device get to encrypted data, so people and organizations using affected Microsoft software need the updates to reduce real-world risk.

    Summary
    Microsoft’s July 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes a record 570 vulnerabilities, including 59 critical flaws and three zero-days. Two of the zero-days, affecting Active Directory Federation Services and SharePoint Server, were already exploited in attacks, making rapid patching especially urgent.

    Microsoft’s July 2026 Patch Tuesday released security updates for a record-breaking 570 flaws. The fixes include three zero-day vulnerabilities, with two exploited in attacks and one publicly disclosed. The update addresses 59 vulnerabilities rated Critical, including 48 remote code execution flaws, 9 elevation of privilege flaws, 1 security bypass flaw, and 1 spoofing flaw.

    The two actively exploited zero-days are CVE-2026-56155 in Active Directory Federation Services and CVE-2026-56164 in Microsoft SharePoint Server. The AD FS flaw allows an authorized attacker to elevate privileges locally, while the SharePoint flaw involves missing authentication for a critical function that lets an unauthorized attacker elevate privileges over a network. Microsoft said enabling AMSI on the SharePoint server and setting Request Body Scan mode to Full can help mitigate CVE-2026-56164.

    Microsoft also patched CVE-2026-50661, a publicly disclosed Windows BitLocker security feature bypass vulnerability. The company said an attacker with physical access to a target system could exploit it to bypass BitLocker Device Encryption and gain access to encrypted data. The article notes that the 570-flaw count excludes some Microsoft fixes released earlier in the month and excludes 468 Microsoft Edge/Chromium flaws fixed by Google this month.

    • The 570-flaw total is not the full Microsoft ecosystem patch burden for the month, because it excludes issues fixed earlier in Mariner, Azure OpenAI, Azure Synapse, M365 Copilot, Exchange Online, Edge for Android, Entra Provisioning Service, and 468 Edge/Chromium flaws fixed by Google.
    • Microsoft had warned that Patch Tuesday update volume would increase because it is using an AI-powered vulnerability discovery system to find more Windows flaws before attackers can exploit them.
    • The Active Directory Federation Services zero-day was credited to Microsoft DART, which the article says indicates it was likely uncovered while investigating active attacks.
    • The actively exploited SharePoint Server zero-day is listed as only Moderate severity in the vulnerability table, but Microsoft still provided a specific mitigation: enable AMSI and set Request Body Scan mode to Full.
    Key Points
    • 01Microsoft’s July 2026 Patch Tuesday released security updates for a record-breaking 570 flaws, including three zero-day vulnerabilities.
    • 02The updates address 59 critical vulnerabilities, including 48 remote code execution flaws, 9 elevation of privilege flaws, 1 security bypass flaw, and 1 spoofing flaw.
    • 03Two actively exploited zero-days were patched: CVE-2026-56155 in Active Directory Federation Services and CVE-2026-56164 in Microsoft SharePoint Server.
    • 04Microsoft also patched CVE-2026-50661, a publicly disclosed Windows BitLocker security feature bypass vulnerability that could allow an attacker with physical access to gain access to encrypted data.
    • 05Microsoft said enabling AMSI on SharePoint Server and setting Request Body Scan mode to Full can help mitigate CVE-2026-56164.

    In plain words

    Microsoft released its July 2026 security update fixing 622 problems across products such as Windows, Office, SharePoint, Exchange Server, SQL Server, Microsoft Defender, Copilot, Dynamics, Minecraft Bedrock Dedicated Server and Microsoft cloud services. Two of the problems had already been used by attackers in the real world, including issues in Active Directory Federation Services and SharePoint Server. Many of the most serious problems could let attackers run their own code, gain higher access, fake actions or bypass protections, so organizations using these Microsoft products need the updates to reduce the chance of compromise. Cisco Talos also released Snort detection rules to help spot attempts to abuse some of these problems.

    Summary
    Microsoft’s July 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes 622 vulnerabilities, including 57 critical issues and two flaws already exploited in the wild affecting AD FS and SharePoint Server. Cisco Talos released updated Snort rules to help detect exploitation attempts for several of these vulnerabilities.

    Microsoft released its July 2026 monthly security update, addressing 622 vulnerabilities across a wide range of products. Microsoft marked 57 of the vulnerabilities as critical, including 48 remote code execution issues, seven elevation of privilege issues, one spoofing issue and one security feature bypass issue. Microsoft also noted that two vulnerabilities disclosed this month have been exploited in the wild: CVE-2026-56155 in Active Directory Federation Services and CVE-2026-56164 in Microsoft SharePoint Server.

    The critical remote code execution vulnerabilities affect products and services including Windows Media and Media Foundation, Windows DHCP client and DHCP Server, Microsoft Office, SharePoint, SQL Server, Windows TCP/IP, Print Spooler, Active Directory Domain Services, Microsoft Defender, Copilot, Dynamics and Minecraft Bedrock Dedicated Server. Eleven of the critical remote code execution vulnerabilities are rated “more likely” to be exploited, including issues involving heap-based buffer overflows, use-after-free, race conditions and deserialization flaws. The article also highlights many important-severity vulnerabilities that Microsoft rated as more likely to be exploited, mostly involving elevation of privilege across Windows components and related services.

    Cisco Talos is releasing a new Snort ruleset to detect attempts to exploit some of the disclosed vulnerabilities. The article states that additional rules may be released later and that current rules may change as more information becomes available. It lists Snort 2 rule ranges 1:66733–1:66743, 1:66745–1:66785, 1:66791–1:66793 and 1:66800–1:66807, along with Snort 3 rules 1:301555–1:301579 and 1:301581–1:301583.

    • The two vulnerabilities Microsoft says were exploited in the wild are not among the 57 critical entries, showing that the article’s most urgent issues are not limited to Microsoft’s highest severity label.
    • Microsoft Office, Word and PowerPoint account for many of the remaining critical remote code execution vulnerabilities, and the article notes these are typically triggered by opening a specially crafted document.
    • Several critical cloud-service entries, including Copilot, Azure Synapse, Azure OpenAI, Exchange Online and Entra items, do not have Microsoft exploitation-likelihood ratings, unlike many of the on-premises product vulnerabilities discussed in the article.
    • The article separates a large set of important-severity vulnerabilities as worth highlighting because Microsoft rates their exploitation as more likely, making exploitability a major prioritization factor alongside severity.
    • Cisco Talos released both Snort 2 and Snort 3 rule ranges for this Patch Tuesday, indicating detection coverage is available but may change as more information becomes available.
    Key Points
    • 01Microsoft’s July 2026 security update includes 622 vulnerabilities across multiple products, with 57 marked as critical.
    • 02Microsoft said two vulnerabilities disclosed this month, CVE-2026-56155 in Active Directory Federation Services and CVE-2026-56164 in Microsoft SharePoint Server, have been exploited in the wild.
    • 03The 57 critical vulnerabilities include 48 remote code execution issues, seven elevation of privilege issues, one spoofing issue and one security feature bypass issue.
    • 04Eleven of the critical remote code execution vulnerabilities are rated by Microsoft as more likely to be exploited and affect products including Windows DHCP Server, Windows DHCP client, Windows Media and Media Foundation, Microsoft Message Queuing, SharePoint, Dynamics and Minecraft Bedrock Dedicated Server.
    • 05Cisco Talos is releasing a new Snort ruleset to detect attempts to exploit some of the disclosed vulnerabilities, including listed Snort 2 and Snort 3 rule ranges.

    In plain words

    Microsoft released a Windows 10 security update called KB5099539 for people and organizations using Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC or devices enrolled in Microsoft’s extended security update program. It includes fixes from the July 2026 Patch Tuesday release, covering 570 security problems, including flaws that were already being used or publicly known. This matters because enrolled Windows 10 devices can keep getting important protection until October 12, 2027, but some older apps that rely on certain unregistered third-party networking components may stop working after the update.

    Summary
    Microsoft released the Windows 10 KB5099539 extended security update with July 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes for 570 vulnerabilities, available to Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC and ESU-enrolled devices. The update also fixes several known issues but may break legacy apps using unregistered third-party TDI transports due to new security hardening.

    Microsoft has released the Windows 10 KB5099539 extended security update for Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC and devices enrolled in the Windows 10 Extended Security Updates program. The update includes the July 2026 Patch Tuesday security updates for 570 vulnerabilities, along with additional security fixes. Microsoft previously extended its free Windows 10 ESU program for consumers by an additional year, allowing enrolled devices to receive security updates until October 12, 2027.

    After installing KB5099539, Windows 10 is updated to build 19045.7548, and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 is updated to build 19044.7548. Microsoft is no longer releasing new features for Windows 10, so this update primarily contains security updates and bug fixes. The fixes include issues affecting OLE Automation, File Explorer, the Recycle Bin, input hotkey behavior, Secure Boot, networking, and Remote Desktop security.

    Microsoft warns that a security hardening change enforcing TDI transport registration requirements may cause applications using unregistered third-party TDI transports to stop working after installation. Users can check whether they are affected by looking in the Windows System event log in Event Viewer for AFD Event ID 16003 entries. Microsoft says there are otherwise no known issues with this update.

    • Organizations can proactively identify systems affected by the TDI hardening change by checking the Windows System event log for AFD Event ID 16003 entries that mention an unregistered TDI provider.
    • IT administrators should migrate trusted Remote Desktop publisher thumbprints to SHA-256 or a stronger algorithm because SHA-1 support is retained only for backward compatibility and is planned for future removal.
    • The update corrects a June 2026 security update compatibility issue in OLE Automation that could cause failures in applications using IDispatch::Invoke with BYREF parameters sharing the same underlying storage.
    • If certain built-in Windows keyboard shortcuts temporarily stop responding after the update, Microsoft says restarting the affected app will typically resolve the issue.
    Key Points
    • 01Microsoft released the Windows 10 KB5099539 extended security update, which includes the July 2026 Patch Tuesday security updates for 570 vulnerabilities and additional security fixes.
    • 02Consumers enrolled in Microsoft’s free Windows 10 Extended Security Updates program can receive security updates until October 12, 2027, after Microsoft extended the program by an additional year.
    • 03Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC users and devices enrolled in the ESU program can install KB5099539 through Windows Update by manually checking for updates.
    • 04After installing KB5099539, Windows 10 is updated to build 19045.7548 and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 is updated to build 19044.7548.
    • 05Microsoft warns that a security hardening change enforcing TDI transport registration requirements may cause legacy applications using unregistered third-party TDI transports to stop working.

    In plain words

    Microsoft released required updates for Windows 11 versions 25H2, 24H2, and 23H2 to fix security problems, bugs, and add some new features. This matters for people and organizations using Windows 11 because the updates include fixes for 571 security weaknesses, along with improvements like more reliable Bluetooth connections, faster AirPods pairing, and better file, network, printing, and accessibility features. Microsoft says it is not aware of any new problems caused by this month’s update.

    Summary
    Microsoft released mandatory Windows 11 cumulative updates KB5101650 and KB5099414 for versions 25H2/24H2 and 23H2, including July 2026 Patch Tuesday security fixes for 571 vulnerabilities. The updates also add reliability and usability improvements such as faster Bluetooth pairing for AirPods, Point-in-Time restore availability, Widgets changes, File Explorer fixes, and networking, printing, WSL, and accessibility updates.

    Microsoft released the Windows 11 KB5101650 and KB5099414 cumulative updates for versions 25H2/24H2 and 23H2. The updates are mandatory because they include the July 2026 Patch Tuesday security patches for 571 vulnerabilities discovered in previous months. Users can install the updates through Windows Update or manually from the Microsoft Update Catalog.

    After installation, Windows 11 25H2 changes to build 26200.8875, Windows 11 24H2 changes to build 26100.8875, and Windows 11 23H2 changes to build 22631.7376. The release is based on 24H2, so Windows 11 25H2 receives the same update and has no exclusive changes. Microsoft says it is not aware of any new issues with this month’s Patch Tuesday release.

    The updates include Bluetooth-related fixes, including faster and more reliable pairing with AirPods, improved microphone reliability for Beats Studio Pro headphones, and better Bluetooth audio stability. Microsoft is also adding Point-in-Time restore for everyone, with greater control for enterprise customers. Other changes include updates for Widgets, Accessibility, File Explorer, Phone Link call audio routing, networking, printing, WSL, display and graphics, location services, Search, and touchpad input.

    • Windows 11 25H2 and 24H2 receive the same July 2026 update because the release is based on 24H2, so there are no exclusive fixes or features for 25H2 in this Patch Tuesday release.
    • Microsoft is making Point-in-Time restore available to everyone, while enterprise customers will receive greater control over the feature.
    • New printer installations will use Internet Printing Protocol by default when supported, and Microsoft links this change to its plan to deprecate third-party printer drivers on Windows.
    • Some anticipated Windows 11 changes, including a movable taskbar and clutter-free Windows Search, are still only in testing and are not included in this release.
    Key Points

    • 05Microsoft says it is not aware of any new issues with this month’s Patch Tuesday release.

In plain words

Microsoft released its largest monthly security fix ever, covering 622 problems, including two that attackers are already using in SharePoint Server and Active Directory Federation Services. This mainly affects organizations that run their own Microsoft document-sharing servers or login-signing systems, because attackers could use these flaws to gain more power inside those systems. It matters because these are central business tools, and the article warns that teams should fix the already-used flaws first rather than relying only on severity scores.

Summary
Microsoft’s record July Patch Tuesday fixes 622 flaws, including two actively exploited zero-days in on-prem SharePoint Server and Active Directory Federation Services that should be prioritized over higher-scored bugs. The update also brings Kerberos RC4 hardening that may break logins if service accounts are not audited and remediated first.

Microsoft released its largest Patch Tuesday on record, covering 622 of its own CVEs according to its Security Update Guide. Two of the fixes address zero-days already being exploited: CVE-2026-56164 in on-premises SharePoint Server and CVE-2026-56155 in Active Directory Federation Services. Both are elevation-of-privilege flaws in identity and collaboration infrastructure, and the article says they should be patched first even though they are not headline critical remote code execution bugs.

CVE-2026-56164 allows an unauthenticated attacker to escalate privileges over the network on SharePoint Server, and Microsoft notes that enabling AMSI in Full Mode can blunt the attack. The SharePoint issue is especially urgent because SharePoint Server 2016 and 2019 reached the end of extended support the same day, with no paid ESU program mentioned. CVE-2026-56155 affects Active Directory Federation Services and lets an already-authenticated attacker elevate privileges locally through weak access controls.

The release also includes a publicly disclosed BitLocker bypass, CVE-2026-50661, which requires physical access and is not under active attack. Another SharePoint fix, CVE-2026-55040, addresses a JWT authentication bypass that Rapid7 chained with a separate remote code execution bug expected to be fixed in August. The update also completes Microsoft’s Kerberos RC4 hardening by removing a rollback switch, which can cause authentication failures if organizations have not audited and remediated service accounts that still request RC4 tickets.

  • The two actively exploited flaws are not the highest-scored issues in the release, showing that Microsoft’s exploited flag is more useful for triage this month than severity labels alone.
  • The SharePoint zero-day has added urgency because SharePoint Server 2016 and 2019 reached the end of extended support on the same day, and the article says there is no paid ESU program for them.
  • Rapid7’s SharePoint JWT authentication bypass matters even though its severity score is disputed, because it breaks a chain Rapid7 used to reach unauthenticated remote code execution with a second bug Microsoft is expected to patch in August.
  • The Kerberos RC4 hardening is operationally risky rather than breach-driven, because installing the update before auditing and rotating affected service account passwords can cause authentication failures.
  • The record patch volume may reflect Microsoft’s growing use of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery, but the article warns that the same post-patch analysis pressure can shrink defenders’ time to act after updates ship.
Key Points
  • 01Microsoft released its largest Patch Tuesday on record, covering 622 of its own CVEs according to the Security Update Guide.
  • 02Two actively exploited zero-days, CVE-2026-56164 in on-premises SharePoint Server and CVE-2026-56155 in Active Directory Federation Services, are elevation-of-privilege flaws that Microsoft says should be prioritized despite not being headline critical remote code execution bugs.
  • 03CVE-2026-56164 allows an unauthenticated attacker to escalate privileges over the network on SharePoint Server, and Microsoft notes that enabling AMSI in Full Mode can blunt the attack.
  • 04CVE-2026-50661 is a publicly disclosed BitLocker bypass that is not under active attack and requires physical access to the device.
  • 05The July update removes the Kerberos RC4 rollback switch, meaning RC4 works only for accounts explicitly configured to allow it and some service accounts may fail authentication if administrators do not audit and remediate first.

    AsyncAPI npm packages backdoored via GitHub Actions
    aikido.dev · 14 Jul 2026 10:00 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.5
    TAGSaikidoasyncapiasyncapi-generatorasyncapi-specsethereumgithubgithub-actionsipfsm-red-teammiasmanostrnpmprt-scanpull-request-targetrentry
    In plain words

    Attackers broke into the publishing process for five widely used AsyncAPI software packages and added code that runs when those packages are used. The affected packages are downloaded millions of times a week, so developers and build machines that used these exact versions could have silently installed a hidden program that lets someone remotely run commands on the computer. This matters because those computers may hold source code access, cloud logins, publishing tokens, and other sensitive credentials, which the article says should be treated as potentially exposed.

    Summary
    Five AsyncAPI npm packages were backdoored after an attacker stole an npm publish token through a vulnerable GitHub Actions pull_request_target workflow. Importing the affected packages installs a persistent Node.js implant with remote shell access, so users should downgrade, hunt for indicators, and rotate exposed credentials.

    Five trojanized @asyncapi npm packages were published on 2026-07-14 after an attacker stole an npm publish token by exploiting a vulnerable pull_request_target GitHub Actions workflow in the AsyncAPI generator repository. The compromised releases were @asyncapi/specs@6.11.2, @asyncapi/specs@6.11.2-alpha.1, @asyncapi/generator@3.3.1, @asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1, and @asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1. The affected packages collectively receive roughly 2.9 million weekly downloads, with @asyncapi/specs accounting for about 2.7 million.

    The malicious code was placed in normal runtime modules rather than npm lifecycle hooks, so a plain require() could trigger it. Importing an affected package fetched an encrypted Node.js loader from IPFS, wrote it to disk as sync.js, and started it as a detached process. The recovered payload self-identifies as M-RED-TEAM v6.4, uses Miasma-branded paths and artifacts, and ultimately provides a persistent implant with a real remote shell.

    The implant beacons to 85.137.53.71:8080 about every 30 seconds and can execute shell commands, while credential harvesting and self-propagation code are present but disabled in this build. The article says misleading config fields such as safeMode, actualPersist, and canaryPercent do not prevent persistence or remote shell capability in the actual execution path. Users are advised to downgrade to earlier versions, remove compromised versions from manifests, lockfiles, caches, mirrors, and build images, hunt for listed host and network indicators, rotate potentially exposed credentials, and rebuild compromised hosts.

    • The compromise can affect systems that merely imported the packages, not only systems that installed them, because the malicious code was embedded in normal runtime modules rather than npm lifecycle scripts.
    • The config values that appeared to indicate a limited or safe canary deployment were misleading, because the analyzed execution paths ignored safeMode, actualPersist, and canaryPercent while still enabling persistence and remote shell capability.
    • The C2 channel uses HTTP, and the command handler falls back to plaintext commands when encrypted commands are absent, which means an on-path attacker could inject commands through that path.
    • The previously reported fix for the vulnerable pull_request_target workflow had been submitted nearly two months before the attack but remained unmerged when the attacker exploited the issue.
    • One compromised tarball, @asyncapi/specs@6.11.2-alpha.1, was still directly downloadable despite being absent from registry metadata, so cleanup requires purging backing storage and CDN copies as well as registry listings.
    Key Points
    • 01Five trojanized @asyncapi npm packages were published on 2026-07-14 after an attacker stole an npm publish token by exploiting a vulnerable GitHub Actions pull_request_target workflow in the AsyncAPI generator repository.
    • 02The malicious code was placed in normal runtime modules, so importing an affected package was enough to fetch an encrypted Node.js loader from IPFS, write it to disk as sync.js, and start it as a detached process.
    • 03The recovered payload identifies itself in code comments as M-RED-TEAM v6.4 and uses Miasma-branded paths and artifacts, but the article makes no definitive attribution.
    • 04The implant beacons to 85.137.53.71:8080 about every 30 seconds and includes a ShellExec command path that can run arbitrary shell commands with only killall blacklisted.
    • 05The article advises users to downgrade to earlier package versions, remove the compromised versions from manifests and caches, hunt for host and network indicators, rotate exposed credentials from a clean machine, and rebuild compromised hosts.

    Three software packages used by AsyncAPI developers were tampered with so they secretly download and run harmful code when used. People and teams who installed the affected versions, especially in development or automated build systems, may have had passwords, access tokens, cloud keys, SSH keys, or other secrets exposed. The hidden code can keep running on the computer, take commands, handle files, steal credentials, and communicate with outside servers, so affected users are urged to avoid those versions, update when fixes are available, check their systems, and rotate exposed credentials.

    Summary
    Three compromised npm packages in the @asyncapi namespace were found delivering a multi-stage Miasma botnet loader that runs when the packages are imported and persists as a disguised NodeJS sync.js file. Users should avoid the affected versions, upgrade when patched, and review developer and CI systems while rotating exposed credentials.

    Socket’s Threat Research Team identified three compromised npm packages in the @asyncapi namespace distributing a multi-stage botnet loader. The affected packages are @asyncapi/generator-helpers v1.1.1, @asyncapi/generator-components v0.7.1, and @asyncapi/generator v3.3.1. The article says users should avoid the affected versions, upgrade to patched releases when available, and review developer and CI environments for signs of compromise.

    The compromised AsyncAPI packages are used in tooling workflows that generate API documentation and client code from AsyncAPI definitions. Because these packages may be imported during normal development or CI execution, the malicious payload does not require a separate install hook to run. The first-stage payload was injected into src/utils.js, hidden behind a large block of leading whitespace, and executes at require() time.

    Stage 1 launches a detached Node.js child process that downloads an encrypted second-stage payload identified as Miasma from IPFS. The second stage persists as sync.js in platform-specific directories disguised as NodeJS, including locations under macOS, Linux, and Windows user directories. Current findings indicate the decrypted second-stage payload is a botnet framework with capabilities for shell command execution, file operations, credential harvesting, evasion checks, persistence, and multi-protocol command and control.

    • The malicious code can run during normal development or CI use because it executes when the package is imported, so checking only install-time scripts would not be sufficient.
    • The payload was concealed behind a large block of leading whitespace inside a legitimate source file, making source-code diff review and inspection of unusual formatting especially important for these packages.
    • The article recommends treating exposed developer and CI environments as potentially credential-compromised, with npm tokens, GitHub tokens, cloud credentials, SSH keys, and CI secrets specifically called out for rotation.
    • Defenders have concrete places to look for compromise, including unexpected Node.js activity, connections to 85.137.53.71, and changes under .claude, .vscode, .cursorrules, and platform-specific NodeJS application data folders.

In plain words

Attackers got the ability to add code to two AsyncAPI software projects on GitHub and used the projects’ own release systems to publish poisoned versions of four npm packages. People and companies that downloaded and used those specific versions of @asyncapi/generator, @asyncapi/generator-helpers, @asyncapi/generator-components, or @asyncapi/specs could have run hidden code that downloaded Miasma RAT, a tool described as able to steal credentials, run commands, and spread to other machines. This matters because the packages appeared to come from the real projects with valid publishing proof, showing that a “trusted” release can still be dangerous if the account or access used to start it was compromised.

Summary
Attackers compromised push access to two AsyncAPI GitHub repositories and used legitimate GitHub Actions release workflows with npm OIDC provenance to publish malicious package versions containing a Miasma RAT dropper. The key lesson is that valid provenance proves a trusted pipeline built the package, but it does not prove the triggering commit was legitimate.

On July 14, 2026, a coordinated supply chain attack affected two AsyncAPI GitHub repositories and led to malicious npm releases of four packages. The affected versions were @asyncapi/generator@3.3.1, @asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1, @asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1, and @asyncapi/specs@6.11.2, with @asyncapi/specs@6.11.2-alpha.1 also published during the incident. The attacker gained push access to the repositories and used the projects’ legitimate GitHub Actions release workflows to publish the packages via npm’s GitHub OIDC trusted-publisher integration, with no npm token stolen.

The article emphasizes that the packages carried legitimate SLSA provenance attestations, but those attestations only proved that the authorized project workflow produced them. They did not prove that the commits triggering the workflows were legitimate. Both repository compromises used the same placeholder git identity, shared the same Miasma RAT second-stage payload infrastructure, and showed the same drop behavior.

The malicious code was an obfuscated dropper that ran when the poisoned library was loaded, not during package installation. It spawned a hidden detached Node.js process, fetched an IPFS-hosted sync.js payload, wrote it to an OS-specific hidden “NodeJS” directory, and launched it. Static analysis identified the decrypted payload as “Miasma v3,” with capabilities including multiple command-and-control channels, credential harvesting, AI tool poisoning, local network movement, persistence, shell execution, and self-destruct functionality.

  • The packages had legitimate SLSA provenance attestations, but the article emphasizes that this only proved the authorized workflow published them and did not prove the triggering commits were legitimate.
  • The dropper did not use npm install scripts, so defenses focused only on install-time behavior could miss it because it ran when the poisoned library was loaded during normal use.
  • The malicious code was padded with roughly a thousand leading spaces to push it off-screen in GitHub’s diff view, making human review of the commit less likely to notice it.
  • The same placeholder git identity, second-stage infrastructure, and drop behavior across two separate repositories showed the incidents were coordinated rather than isolated package compromises.
  • The Miasma payload included several fallback communication methods, including HTTP, Nostr, IPFS, BitTorrent DHT, libp2p GossipSub, and Ethereum, meaning blocking only the primary C2 endpoint would not fully cut off the implant.
Key Points
  • 01A coordinated supply chain attack on July 14, 2026 compromised two AsyncAPI GitHub repositories and produced malicious npm package versions for @asyncapi/generator, @asyncapi/generator-helpers, @asyncapi/generator-components, and @asyncapi/specs.
  • 02The attacker gained push access to the repositories and used the projects’ legitimate GitHub Actions release pipelines with npm GitHub OIDC trusted-publisher integration, so no npm token was stolen.
  • 03The malicious packages carried an obfuscated dropper that executed when the library was loaded during normal use, not during npm installation.
  • 04Static analysis showed the dropper fetched an IPFS-hosted second-stage sync.js payload and installed it in hidden OS-specific NodeJS directories before launching it detached and hidden.
  • 05The decrypted second-stage payload was identified as Miasma v3 and included multiple command-and-control channels, credential harvesting, persistence, lateral movement, shell execution, and self-destruct capabilities.

In plain words

SonicWall says attackers are already using two newly fixed weaknesses in its SMA1000 products to target affected devices. The affected customers are organizations using SMA1000 models 6210, 7210, and 8200v with specific software versions, while SonicWall says its firewall SSL-VPN and SMA 100 Series products are not affected. This matters because attackers may be able to make these devices contact unintended places or run commands on them, and U.S. officials have ordered federal agencies to fix affected systems by July 17, 2026, or stop using them.

Summary
SonicWall says two SMA1000 flaws, CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410, are being actively exploited in zero-day attacks and urges customers to install the latest hotfix immediately. Compromised devices should be re-imaged or redeployed, with passwords and TOTP tokens reset.

SonicWall warned that threat actors are actively exploiting two SMA1000 vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410, in zero-day attacks. The company investigated multiple incidents and confirmed exploitation of both flaws. SonicWall urged customers to install newly released hotfixes as soon as possible.

CVE-2026-15409 is a critical server-side request forgery vulnerability in the SMA1000 Appliance Work Place interface that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to force an appliance to make requests to unintended locations. CVE-2026-15410 is a high-severity post-authentication code injection flaw in the SMA1000 Appliance Management Console that could allow a remote authenticated administrator to execute arbitrary operating system commands. SonicWall has not disclosed whether attackers are chaining the two vulnerabilities together.

The vulnerabilities affect SMA1000 models 6210, 7210, and 8200v running specific platform-hotfix releases, with fixes available in versions 12.4.3-03453 and 12.5.0-02835 and later. SonicWall said there are no workarounds or mitigations other than installing the hotfixes, and advised re-imaging or redeploying compromised appliances, changing user and administrator passwords, and resetting TOTP tokens. CISA added both vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and gave federal agencies until July 17, 2026, to secure affected systems or discontinue use if mitigations cannot be applied.

  • SonicWall says there are no workarounds or mitigations for these flaws other than installing the hotfixes, making patching the only stated remediation path for affected devices.
  • SonicWall’s compromise guidance goes beyond patching: if an appliance is found compromised, administrators are advised to re-image physical appliances or redeploy virtual appliances, change all user and administrator passwords, and reset TOTP tokens.
  • Although CVE-2026-15410 requires administrator privileges, SonicWall assigned the overall advisory a maximum CVSS score of 10.0.
  • SonicWall provided specific indicators of compromise in log files and configuration paths, including unexpected requests to /__api__/login or /__api__/logout and suspicious /wsproxy host parameters.

In plain words

The article says at least two attacker groups are using a new trick against Microsoft Entra ID, a Microsoft cloud login system, to check whether stolen usernames and passwords are real without creating the normal warning signs defenders rely on. The campaigns targeted millions of user accounts across thousands of organizations, using cloud services from Amazon Web Services and Cloudflare as part of their activity. This matters because attackers can quietly find working accounts for later break-ins, while organizations may miss the activity because it is hidden among fake application identifiers rather than appearing as normal login records.

Summary
Proofpoint reports that threat actors are using OAuth client ID spoofing against Microsoft Entra ID to enumerate accounts and validate stolen passwords without generating normal successful sign-in telemetry. Two large campaigns used millions of spoofed app IDs across thousands of tenants, making detection harder because activity is fragmented across fictional applications.

At least two threat actors are using a technique called OAuth client ID spoofing in cloud campaigns against Microsoft Entra ID environments. Proofpoint said the activity lets attackers enumerate user accounts and validate stolen credentials without generating a successful sign-in event that would normally alert defenders. The technique creates a blind spot because Entra ID returns different error responses depending on whether a supplied OAuth client ID is valid.

The attacks use spoofed OAuth client IDs in HTTP POST requests to Microsoft’s OAuth 2.0 token endpoint through the Resource Owner Password Credentials flow. In these cases, Entra sign-in logs record only the application ID without a corresponding application name, which can cause detections based on surges against a specific application name to miss the activity. Proofpoint said attackers can use the resulting AADSTS error codes to infer whether an account exists and whether a password is correct.

Proofpoint identified two large campaigns that adopted the technique toward the end of December 2025. UNK_pyreq2323 used more than 700,000 spoofed client IDs from AWS infrastructure to target more than 1 million accounts across nearly 4,000 tenants, causing lockouts for roughly 28% of targeted users. UNK_OutFlareAZ used Cloudflare infrastructure to target over 2 million users with 3.7 million randomized spoofed application IDs.

  • Detections that rely on spikes against a specific application name may fail because spoofed client IDs leave the application name field blank in Entra sign-in logs.
  • Conditional Access policies scoped only to commonly targeted applications may not mitigate this activity because spoofed client IDs do not trigger policies tied to a specific application.
  • The two campaigns used different spoofing patterns, with UNK_pyreq2323 modifying trailing digits of a known application ID and reusing IDs across up to 12 users, while UNK_OutFlareAZ generated a unique client ID per request.
  • The UNK_pyreq2323 campaign caused lockouts for roughly 28% of targeted users, showing that this stealth-focused technique can still create visible operational disruption.
Key Points
  • 01At least two threat actors are using OAuth client ID spoofing in cloud campaigns to enumerate Microsoft Entra ID user accounts and validate stolen credentials without generating a successful sign-in event.
  • 02Proofpoint said the technique abuses differences in Entra ID error responses when spoofed OAuth client IDs are supplied to Microsoft’s OAuth 2.0 token endpoint using the Resource Owner Password Credentials flow.
  • 03When spoofed client IDs are used, Entra sign-in logs record the application ID without a corresponding application name, which can cause detections based on specific application names to miss the activity.
  • 04Proofpoint identified UNK_pyreq2323 as a campaign from January to March 2026 that used more than 700,000 spoofed client IDs from AWS infrastructure to target more than 1 million accounts across nearly 4,000 tenants.
  • 05Proofpoint identified UNK_OutFlareAZ as a campaign starting in December 2025 that used Cloudflare infrastructure to target over 2 million users with 3.7 million randomized spoofed application IDs.

    In plain words

    The U.S. government sanctioned a private internet service called First VPN Service, its administrator, and a Belarusian seller of tools that helped criminals hide harmful software from security programs. Officials say these services helped ransomware groups hide who they were and carry out attacks against U.S. businesses, hospitals, financial firms, and local governments. This matters because the attacks caused billions of dollars in losses and affected critical services people rely on, so the U.S. and its partners are trying to cut off not just the attackers but also the people and services that make their crimes possible.

    Summary
    The U.S. sanctioned First VPN Service, its administrator, and a Belarusian cryptor seller for helping ransomware groups hide identities, evade detection, and attack U.S. organizations. The action follows an international law enforcement takedown of 1VPNS infrastructure tied to ransomware, fraud, and other cybercrime worldwide.

    The U.S. Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned First VPN Service, also known as 1VPNS, its administrator Dmytro Rashevskyi, and Belarusian national Yegeniy Vladimirovich Silayev for enabling ransomware attacks against U.S. organizations. OFAC said 1VPNS sold services to ransomware groups, while Silayev sold cryptors that helped ransomware and other malware evade detection by security software. Under the sanctions, property of the designated individuals and entities within U.S. jurisdiction is blocked, and U.S. persons and businesses are barred from transactions involving them.

    According to the article, 1VPNS had advertised on cybercriminal forums since 2014 that it kept no logs of user activity or identities and would not cooperate with law enforcement. Rashevskyi allegedly used false identities, including “Maksim Sorin” and “Roman Chabanenko,” to acquire infrastructure from companies that would otherwise have refused service because of abuse complaints. Victims of ransomware attacks involving 1VPNS infrastructure included U.S. businesses, hospitals, financial services firms, and municipal governments.

    The sanctions followed a May law enforcement takedown of 1VPNS’s website and infrastructure during Operation Saffron, led by French and Dutch authorities with support from the FBI’s Boston Field Office. Authorities said the investigation began in December 2021 and involved infiltrating the VPN’s infrastructure and collecting its user database before dismantling it. Officials seized 33 servers across 27 countries, arrested the administrator, and exposed thousands of users associated with ransomware, fraud, and other malicious activity, while estimating that ransomware operations using 1VPNS and Silayev cryptors caused billions of dollars in losses in the United States.

    • The sanctions target not only ransomware operators but also the infrastructure and tool providers that make ransomware operations harder to trace and detect.
    • Law enforcement had infiltrated 1VPNS infrastructure and collected its user database before dismantling the service, showing that the takedown produced intelligence on thousands of suspected malicious users.
    • Rashevskyi allegedly used false identities to acquire infrastructure from companies that would otherwise have refused service because of abuse complaints, highlighting how service providers can be deceived into supporting criminal infrastructure.
    • Europol said 1VPNS had appeared in nearly every major cybercrime investigation it supported, indicating the service had become a recurring enabler across many separate criminal cases.
    • The sanctions were coordinated with the United Kingdom and followed European law enforcement action, reflecting a combined legal, financial, and operational approach against ransomware support networks.
    Key Points
    • 01The U.S. Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned First VPN Service, its administrator Dmytro Rashevskyi, and Belarusian national Yegeniy Vladimirovich Silayev for enabling ransomware attacks against U.S. organizations.
    • 02First VPN Service had advertised on cybercriminal forums since 2014 that it kept no logs of user activity or identities and would not cooperate with law enforcement.

In plain words

The U.S. punished a service called First VPN Service, its Ukrainian administrator, and a Belarusian seller of software used to hide harmful programs because officials say they helped criminals carry out ransomware attacks and cover their tracks. Those attacks affected U.S. businesses, financial companies, hospitals, and local governments, causing major financial losses. At the same time, the U.K. and E.U. punished Russian-linked cyber networks accused of disruptive activity across Europe, while U.S. agencies warned that Russian state-backed actors are targeting poorly secured internet equipment around the world.

Summary
The U.S. sanctioned First VPN Service, its Ukrainian administrator, and a Belarusian cryptor seller for helping ransomware and malware operators hide their activity, while the U.K. and E.U. separately sanctioned Russian cyber networks tied to GRU and FSB operations. The actions coincide with new warnings that FSB Center 16 is exploiting poorly configured routers and Cisco vulnerabilities to target critical infrastructure worldwide.

The U.S. Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control designated First VPN Service, its Ukrainian administrator Dmytro Rashevskyi, and Belarusian national Yegeniy Vladimirovich Silayev for enabling ransomware actors and other cybercriminals. First VPN Service was accused of providing tools to ransomware groups, while Silayev was sanctioned for selling cryptors used to disguise ransomware and other malware as safe programs. First VPN was dismantled in May 2026 through a joint European and North American law enforcement operation after allegedly helping criminal actors hide the origins of ransomware attacks, data theft, scanning, and denial-of-service attacks.

The Treasury said several ransomware groups used First VPN to attack U.S. companies and institutions, deploy malware, and manage stolen data. Victims included U.S. businesses, financial services companies, hospitals, and municipal governments. U.S. officials said ransomware groups using services supplied by the sanctioned parties caused billions of dollars in losses to American businesses and critical infrastructure providers. The department also said Rashevskyi used false identities, including “Maksim Sorin” and “Roman Chabanenko,” to buy infrastructure from companies that might otherwise refuse to work with him because of abuse complaints tied to 1VPNS servers.

The article also describes U.K. and E.U. sanctions against 24 Russian individuals and entities linked to destructive cyber and hybrid operations, including GRU leadership, FSB Centre 16, and actors behind Lumma Stealer. Separately, the FBI warned that FSB Center 16 actors are exploiting poorly configured and vulnerable networking devices worldwide, especially routers with active SNMP agents accepting common or default community strings. The advisory said the actors use scans involving spoofed IP addresses and object identifiers that instruct devices to copy configurations and transfer them to attacker-controlled or compromised servers. The activity also involves Cisco vulnerabilities CVE-2018-0171 and CVE-2008-4128, with CISA adding CVE-2008-4128 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

It allows an authenticated attacker to leverage logical errors in memory management and cause memory corruption that could lead to unauthorized data access, data modification, or system unavailability.

SAP also addressed two other critical vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-27690 in SAP Approuter deployments in non-Cloud Foundry environments and CVE-2026-44761 in SAP Commerce Cloud. The article says there is no evidence of exploitation in the wild, but customers are advised to apply the necessary updates.

  • Customers who removed the sample OAuth 2.0 client or replaced its secret with a strong, unique value are not impacted by CVE-2026-44761.

In plain words

Microsoft says attackers linked to ShinyHunters got into company Salesforce systems over the past year by abusing trusted app connections, stolen access from software vendors, and public-facing site settings that were left too open. Companies in retail, education, manufacturing, and major firms using vendors like Salesloft, Gainsight, and Klue were affected or exposed. This matters because the attackers did not need to break Salesforce itself; they used permissions companies had already granted, which can make the activity look normal while customer and business data is copied.

Summary
Microsoft says ShinyHunters-linked actors spent the past year breaching Salesforce environments not through Salesforce flaws, but by abusing trusted OAuth apps, stolen vendor tokens, and misconfigured guest access. The key defense is to monitor connected-app behavior and permissions, remove unused integrations, and tighten Salesforce event logging and guest access controls.

Microsoft reported that attackers whose methods align with the data-extortion group ShinyHunters spent the past year accessing corporate Salesforce environments without exploiting a flaw in Salesforce itself. The campaigns ran from mid-2025 into mid-2026 and affected tenants in industries including retail, education, and manufacturing. Microsoft mapped the activity to three intrusion paths: vishing calls that tricked employees into approving malicious connected apps, stolen OAuth tokens from compromised software vendors, and misconfigured guest access to Salesforce sites.

The first path involved callers posing as IT support and guiding employees through Salesforce’s OAuth consent screen to approve an attacker-controlled connected app disguised as Salesforce Data Loader. The second path involved compromised vendors such as Salesloft Drift, Gainsight, and Klue, where attackers used stolen OAuth tokens or secrets from trusted integrations to reach downstream Salesforce customer environments. The third path involved suspicious guest-user activity against Salesforce Aura endpoints, where misconfigured guest permissions allowed unauthenticated access to data through Aura functionality.

The article emphasizes that these intrusions are hard to catch because approved apps and trusted integrations can make API activity look like normal use, while sign-in and authentication monitoring may show little. Microsoft worked with Salesforce to add Defender for Cloud Apps and Salesforce Shield Event Monitoring capabilities that surface connected-app attribution, OAuth scopes, session context, and API activity. Microsoft’s guidance includes inventorying connected apps, removing unused integrations, applying least privilege, monitoring Salesforce event logs, locking down Experience Cloud guest access, and revoking or rotating tokens when integrations behave unusually.

  • The campaigns were difficult to detect because access through an approved connected app or trusted integration can appear as ordinary Salesforce use, while sign-in and authentication logs may show little or nothing suspicious.
  • The attackers repeatedly searched Salesforce data for credentials and secrets that could unlock other SaaS platforms, making CRM data a stepping stone to broader compromise rather than just the final target.
  • Forgotten or inactive access was a recurring weakness, including unused connected apps with live permissions and Klue’s long-disused legacy credential from a test integration that was never deployed.
  • Salesforce activity visibility needs to focus on what an app does after access is granted, including which connected app made API calls, what scopes it holds, and whether its query volume is normal for the tenant.
  • Misconfigured Salesforce guest access allowed unauthenticated actors to use Aura functionality and cursor-based pagination to pull more records than the standard 2,000-record query limit would normally allow.
Key Points
  • 01Microsoft reported that attackers whose methods align with ShinyHunters accessed corporate Salesforce environments from mid-2025 into mid-2026 without exploiting a Salesforce platform flaw.
  • 02Microsoft grouped the activity into three intrusion paths: vishing calls that tricked employees into approving malicious connected apps, stolen OAuth tokens from compromised software vendors, and misconfigured guest access to Salesforce sites.
  • 03The vendor-token path included the Salesloft Drift compromise, the Gainsight incident, and the Klue compromise, each involving trusted integrations used to access downstream Salesforce customer environments.
  • 04Microsoft and Salesforce added new Defender for Cloud Apps and Salesforce Shield Event Monitoring capabilities to surface connected-app attribution, OAuth scopes, session context, and API activity.
  • 05Microsoft advised organizations to inventory connected apps, remove unused integrations, apply least privilege, monitor Salesforce event logs, tighten Experience Cloud guest-user access, and revoke or rotate tokens when integrations behave unusually.

Dutch intelligence agencies warned that Russian state-backed hackers are systematically compromising internet-connected security cameras across Europe and Ukraine. The Netherlands’ AIVD and MIVD said at least one Russian intelligence service is targeting cameras in the Netherlands, other NATO and EU member states, and Ukraine. The goal is to gather military intelligence, including activity on military transport routes and weapons shipments destined for Ukraine.

In Ukraine, the agencies said hacked cameras have in some cases been used to locate Ukrainian military personnel, with the intelligence later supporting attempts to kill soldiers and destroy equipment. They then automatically analyze video feeds with image-recognition software to identify military vehicles and cargo. The advisory urged organizations operating internet-connected cameras to change default credentials, keep firmware updated, review configurations, and consider cameras’ country of origin.

In plain words

xAI’s Grok Build coding tool was found sending whole saved code projects, including past versions, to xAI storage, not just the files it needed for a task. This could affect developers who used the tool, especially if their projects contained private company code, internal links, customer data, or passwords that were saved now or in the past. xAI appears to have turned the uploads off through a server setting, but it has not fully explained why this happened, how long the data was kept, or how many users were affected.

Summary
xAI’s Grok Build CLI was found uploading entire tracked Git repositories, including commit history and files it never read, to xAI-controlled Google Cloud Storage despite the model-training opt-out being disabled. xAI appears to have shut the behavior off server-side, but users who ran the tool should rotate any credentials that may have been in read files, tracked files, or Git history.

xAI’s Grok Build coding CLI was found uploading entire tracked Git repositories, including full commit history, to an xAI-run Google Cloud Storage bucket rather than only the files needed for a coding task. A researcher publishing as cereblab tested version 0.2.93, captured one of the uploads, cloned the Git bundle from the intercepted request, and recovered a file the agent had been told not to open. The article states that the captures establish transmission, acceptance, and storage, but do not show that xAI trained on the code.

The technical evidence included a 12 GB repository where model-turn traffic to /v1/responses was about 192 KB, while the storage channel to /v1/storage sent 5.10 GiB in 73 chunks of about 75 MB. The destination bucket, grok-code-session-traces, appeared in the binary and in a staged metadata.json with per-file paths pointing to gs://grok-code-session-traces/. The article also says that when Grok read a tracked .env file, fake API_KEY and DB_PASSWORD values were sent unredacted in the model turn and also landed in a session_state archive bound for storage.

Turning off “Improve the model” did not stop the repository uploads, because that setting governed model training rather than whether code left the machine. On July 13, the same 0.2.93 client stopped making storage requests after server settings returned disable_codebase_upload: true and trace_upload_enabled: false, but xAI had not confirmed whether the change applied to every account or was permanent. The article advises anyone who already ran the tool to rotate credentials that Grok could have sent, including anything it read, anything in tracked files, and anything in Git history.

  • The “Improve the model” opt-out did not control whether code left the machine, showing that a training opt-out and a data-upload control were separate settings in Grok Build.
  • Because the captured bundle included Git history, secrets or sensitive files that had been committed and later deleted could still have been uploaded.
  • xAI’s apparent fix was server-side rather than a client update, and a separate analysis found the upload code still present in build 0.2.99, meaning the behavior was controlled remotely by server flags.
  • Users who ran Grok Build may need to rotate credentials not only from files the agent read, but also from tracked files and past commits contained in repository history.
  • The article distinguishes between transmission and storage versus training, noting that the captures establish code was sent to and accepted by xAI storage but do not show that it was used for model training.
Key Points
  • 01A researcher testing Grok Build version 0.2.93 found that the CLI uploaded entire tracked Git repositories, including full commit history, to an xAI-controlled Google Cloud Storage bucket rather than only files needed for a coding task.
  • 02In one test on a 12 GB repository, traffic to the model endpoint was about 192 KB while the storage channel sent 5.10 GiB to /v1/storage in 73 chunks of about 75 MB each.
  • 03The researcher recovered a file named src/_probe/never_read_canary.txt from the captured Git bundle even though the agent had been explicitly told not to open it, and the result was replicated on a second unrelated repository.
  • 04Turning off the “Improve the model” setting did not stop the repository uploads, while the server response still returned trace_upload_enabled: true.
  • 05On July 13, the same 0.2.93 client stopped making storage requests after server-side settings changed to disable_codebase_upload: true and trace_upload_enabled: false, but xAI had not confirmed whether the change applied to every account or was permanent.

Two new phishing kits, Jalisco and OmegaLord, are targeting Microsoft 365 accounts with methods designed to bypass MFA, including real-time device-code phishing and credential/phone-number theft. Defenders should restrict device registration and block or limit device-code authentication to reduce account takeover risk.

Two new phishing kits, Jalisco and OmegaLord, have been discovered in attacks targeting Microsoft 365 accounts. ReliaQuest researchers analyzed both toolkits and said they use techniques intended to defeat multi-factor authentication. Jalisco uses device-code phishing, while OmegaLord masquerades as a PDF reader to collect account login credentials and associated phone numbers.

Jalisco abuses the OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant flow by tricking victims into authorizing an attacker-controlled device through a legitimate Microsoft login page. The toolkit generates fresh Microsoft OAuth device codes automatically when a victim opens the phishing page, bypassing Microsoft’s 15-minute validity window for device codes. ReliaQuest said attackers have registered up to five rogue devices on a single compromised account, sometimes using names containing “Microsoft” or “Windows” to lower suspicion.

After compromising an account, attackers search SharePoint and other SaaS services for valuable data and can exfiltrate it within minutes. ReliaQuest said sensitive data can include customer or employee personally identifiable information, financial records, and internal communications, with exfiltration occurring in as little as six minutes before defenders identify the breach. The researchers recommend reducing the Entra ID device-registration limit, blocking device code authentication through Microsoft Entra Conditional Access, restricting the OAuth Device Authorization grant in Okta, and auditing unnecessary app registrations.

  • Jalisco’s real-time generation of device codes specifically undermines Microsoft’s 15-minute device-code validity limit, showing that time-limited codes alone are not sufficient to stop this phishing method.
  • ReliaQuest’s recommendation to reduce the Entra ID device-registration limit from the default of 50 to one or two is a concrete way to limit the impact of account hijacking and speed remediation.
  • Attackers naming rogue devices with terms like “Microsoft” or “Windows” indicates they are trying to make unauthorized device registrations blend in with legitimate activity.
  • The theft of phone numbers by OmegaLord shows that attackers are targeting information beyond passwords because it may help them intercept or hijack MFA requests or codes.
  • ReliaQuest observed data exfiltration occurring in as little as six minutes, meaning compromised accounts may be abused before defenders have identified the breach.
Key Points
  • 01ReliaQuest researchers discovered two phishing kits, Jalisco and OmegaLord, being used in attacks targeting Microsoft 365 accounts and designed to defeat multi-factor authentication.
  • 02Jalisco uses device-code phishing by generating fresh Microsoft OAuth device codes in real time when a victim opens the phishing page, bypassing Microsoft’s 15-minute code validity limit.
  • 03ReliaQuest said attackers have registered up to five rogue devices on a single compromised account, sometimes using names containing “Microsoft” or “Windows” to appear less suspicious.
  • 04After compromising an account, attackers search SharePoint and other SaaS services for sensitive data and can exfiltrate it in as little as six minutes before issuing extortion demands.
  • 05OmegaLord uses a fake PDF Reader login page to steal email addresses, passwords, and phone numbers, which ReliaQuest said could help attackers bypass MFA protections.

A threat actor created nearly 300 fake GitHub repositories impersonating legitimate software projects to trick users into downloading BoryptGrab infostealer malware. The malware steals browser data, crypto wallet information, messaging tokens, credentials, and files, then exfiltrates them to a Russia-based command-and-control server.

A threat actor published 292 fake GitHub repositories impersonating legitimate software and security projects to distribute infostealer malware. Arctic Wolf identified the activity after finding that one of its products was impersonated starting June 26. The campaign drew traffic from searches for security products, cryptocurrency services, financial tools, developer utilities, secure email providers, macOS utilities, and gaming software.

Each fake repository included a README file with a download link leading to a malicious landing page that used trustworthy wording, branding, and spoofed trust badges. Arctic Wolf found that the delivery pages reused a single templated HTML and JavaScript artifact across all impersonated brands. The page delivered a large ZIP archive whose name and payload changed roughly every minute, containing a trojanized libcurl.dll and a legitimate signed WinGUP updater.

When the user ran the executable, the renamed WinGUP updater side-loaded libcurl.dll, which decoded and reflectively executed an embedded BoryptGrab-lineage infostealer in memory. The malware targeted data from 19 web browsers, 32 cryptocurrency wallet brands, Telegram, Discord, Steam, Meta’s Max messaging application, Windows Credential Manager, and files suggesting passwords, recovery phrases, wallets, or backups. Arctic Wolf said the stolen data was compressed and sent to a Russia-based command-and-control server, and GitHub had removed many of the repositories while several dozen GitHub Pages redirectors remained active at the time of the report.

  • The campaign reused a single templated HTML and JavaScript delivery page across all impersonated brands, with visible branding generated from the URL path.
  • The malicious ZIP archive’s name and payload changed roughly every minute, which could make static blocking based only on file names or hashes less reliable.
  • The BoryptGrab variant included a previously undocumented capability to bypass Chrome’s App-Bound Encryption through direct code injection into the browser process.
  • The malware left forensic evidence behind because it did not wipe the temporary directory used to stage collected data before exfiltration.
  • GitHub had removed many of the fake repositories by the time of Arctic Wolf’s report, but several dozen GitHub Pages redirectors were still active.

In plain words

Researchers found two flaws in RabbitMQ, a service companies use to move messages between applications. The problems affect RabbitMQ versions from 3.13.0 and later and could let outsiders steal a secret needed to take over the system in some setups, or let logged-in users see information about other tenants’ queues. This matters because exposed management systems or shared company environments could reveal messaging details or put control of messages, queues, users, and settings at risk, so RabbitMQ has released fixed versions.

Summary
RabbitMQ has patched two access control flaws that could let attackers leak OAuth client secrets for full broker takeover or let authenticated users view cross-tenant queue and exchange metadata. Organizations running RabbitMQ 3.13.0 or later should update immediately, restrict management interface access, and rotate exposed OAuth secrets.

Cybersecurity researchers disclosed two access control-related flaws affecting the RabbitMQ message broker service. Miggo’s security team discovered and reported the issues, saying one flaw can leak a confidential OAuth secret to an unauthenticated attacker in a single request. The other flaw allows any logged-in user to silently read other tenants’ data.

The flaws have been present in the codebase since early 2024 and affect RabbitMQ release lines from 3.13.0 and later. RabbitMQ has addressed them in versions 4.3.0, 4.2.6, 4.1.11, 4.0.20, and 3.13.15. The article says there is no evidence of active exploitation of either vulnerability before public disclosure.

CVE-2026-57219 involves an obsolete HTTP API endpoint, GET /api/auth, that can reveal a client secret on installations configured with the management.oauth_client_secret key, potentially allowing an attacker to exchange it for an administrator token and take control of messages, queues, users, and broker settings. CVE-2026-57221 is a missing authorization issue that lets any authenticated user connected to a virtual host enumerate queue and exchange names and read queue message and consumer counts regardless of permissions. Users are advised to patch, rotate OAuth client secrets if the management interface is internet-reachable, restrict access to port 15672, separate tenants by virtual host, and block the vulnerable endpoint on unpatched instances.

  • CVE-2026-57219 is especially actionable because an unauthenticated attacker can trigger the leak with a single request when the management port is reachable by an untrusted network.
  • The OAuth secret issue only applies to RabbitMQ installations that configured OAuth 2 using the management.oauth_client_secret key, so defenders can prioritize checking that specific configuration.
  • RabbitMQ operators may need to rotate OAuth client secrets after patching if the management interface was exposed to the internet, because updating alone would not invalidate a secret that may already have been leaked.
  • The second flaw shows that separating tenants only by permissions within the same virtual host may be insufficient, since RabbitMQ specifically recommends separating tenants by virtual host.
  • The disclosed flaws are not the only recent RabbitMQ security concern, as maintainers also addressed critical TLS client-authentication bypass and JWKS-forgery issues that could affect authentication trust.

In plain words

Researchers found 11 old Microsoft-approved startup programs used mainly to help Linux start on modern computers, and these programs can still be trusted by many machines even though they are unsafe. Any computer that trusts Microsoft’s older third-party startup certificate could be affected, no matter what operating system is installed. An attacker who can change the startup process could use one of these old programs to run harmful code before the computer’s normal protections begin, letting it hide deeply and even survive reboots or some system reinstallations.

Summary
Researchers found 11 old Microsoft-signed Linux UEFI shim bootloaders that remain trusted and can let attackers bypass Secure Boot to run code before the operating system loads. Microsoft has revoked the affected shims, but systems must receive the updated Secure Boot revocation list to block their abuse.

Cybersecurity researchers discovered 11 old, Microsoft-signed UEFI shim bootloaders that could be abused to bypass Secure Boot on most systems using the UEFI firmware standard. ESET said an attacker exploiting one of these vulnerable applications can execute untrusted code during system boot, enabling malicious UEFI bootkits or other malware. The issue affects UEFI-based machines that trust Microsoft’s “Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011” third-party UEFI certificate authority certificate, regardless of the installed operating system.

The shim is a lightweight open-source bootloader that helps Linux distributions start when Secure Boot is enabled, with firmware first validating the shim and the shim then validating later boot components. ESET said outdated but trusted shims can allow arbitrary code execution before the operating system loads, including deployment of bootkits such as Bootkitty, HybridPetya, or BlackLotus. Microsoft revoked the impacted shim bootloaders as part of its June 2026 Patch Tuesday update after responsible disclosure earlier in February.

CERT/CC said vendor-specific bootloaders had not been updated after upstream vulnerabilities became public and fixed, leaving vulnerable boot components signed and trusted because they had not been revoked through Microsoft’s DBX revocation list. ESET warned that the expiration of the Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011 certificate does not affect Secure Boot verification unless signed bootloaders are explicitly revoked by hash. Because the code can run before the operating system and security products initialize, the article says it can evade built-in controls and endpoint detection and response tools while enabling persistence across reboots and, in some cases, reinstallation.

  • The risk comes from old but still-trusted signed components rather than a newly discovered flaw, meaning an attacker only needs a copy of a vulnerable unrevoked shim binary and knowledge of how UEFI shims work.
  • The expiration of the Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011 certificate does not by itself stop affected bootloaders from working under Secure Boot, because they must be explicitly revoked by hash.
  • The vulnerable shims can undermine newer protections such as the MOK denylist and Secure Boot Advanced Targeting by allowing older trusted boot components to be reintroduced into the boot chain.
  • Because the malicious code can run before the operating system and security tools start, attacks using these shims may avoid built-in security controls and endpoint detection and response products.
  • CERT/CC described the issue as a long-term supply chain exposure because vendor-specific bootloaders were not updated after upstream shim vulnerabilities became public and fixed.
Key Points
  • 01Cybersecurity researchers discovered 11 old Microsoft-signed UEFI shim bootloaders that could be abused to bypass Secure Boot on most systems using UEFI.
  • 02The vulnerable shim bootloaders affect any UEFI-based machine that trusts Microsoft’s “Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011” third-party UEFI certificate authority certificate, regardless of the installed operating system.
  • 03An attacker with administrative privileges or the ability to modify the boot process could use the vulnerable bootloaders to execute arbitrary code before the operating system loads.
  • 04Microsoft revoked the affected shim bootloaders as part of its June 2026 Patch Tuesday update following responsible disclosure earlier in February.
  • 05ESET warned that the expiration of the Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011 certificate does not affect Secure Boot verification unless bootloaders signed with the expired certificate are explicitly revoked by hash.
